notes: Ruling slot 13 holds MDR-PARMEHUTU. MD's RPF (1987) and Rwanda Defence Force (1994) are anachronistic: slot 20 becomes the Hutu-majoritarian hardliners, slot 22 the Garde Nationale (RDF sprite not reused, different institution). Slot 23 keeps the Nyiginya royal house with its MD sprite. UNAR placed in 6 (monarchist, anti-Western, Eastern-bloc backed).

0.name: Abanyenduga
0.text:
The Abanyenduga are the ministers, prefects and party bosses from Gitarama and the central-southern region of Nduga, home of President Grégoire Kayibanda. Since the 1969 elections they increasingly monopolise ministries, scholarships and state jobs, to the growing anger of the north.

They stand for a strong presidency, close ties with Belgium, the Catholic Church and Western aid donors, and a firm hand against Tutsi exiles and communist influence. Their base is the southern Hutu elite educated in Catholic seminaries, and their leverage rests on their grip over the government, the party apparatus and the distribution of foreign aid.

1.name: Église catholique au Rwanda
1.text:
The Catholic Church in Rwanda is the country's most powerful institution after the state, with a majority of the population baptised and nearly all schools in its hands. It is led by André Perraudin, Archbishop of Kabgayi, whose 1959 Lenten letter supported Hutu emancipation, and Aloys Bigirumwami, Bishop of Nyundo.

The Church stands for Christian social teaching, family morality, Catholic education and close cooperation with Belgium and Western Christian democracy. It trained the Hutu elite that now governs and remains its closest partner. Its leverage lies in its schools, its newspaper Kinyamateka, its hospitals and the loyalty of a deeply Catholic rural population.

2.name: Rassemblement Démocratique Rwandais
2.text:
The Rwandan Democratic Rally was founded in 1959 by moderate Tutsi chiefs and notables around Prosper Bwanakweri who favoured reform and a constitutional monarchy. Favoured at first by the Belgians, it was crushed after the Inyenzi raid of December 1963, when its leaders were executed at Ruhengeri.

RADER stood for gradual democratisation, the rule of law, cooperation between Hutu and Tutsi and close ties with Belgium. In 1970 it survives only as a memory among educated Tutsi who remain inside Rwanda and refuse both exile militancy and Hutu majoritarianism. Its leverage lies in their education and their place in teaching, commerce and the Church.

3.name: Kinyamateka
3.text:
Kinyamateka is the Catholic newspaper founded in 1933, once edited by Grégoire Kayibanda himself, and the voice of the social Catholicism that carried the Hutu revolution. Around it gather Catholic journalists, teachers, cooperative organisers and young Christian workers who still believe in the social promises of 1959.

This milieu calls for land reform, rural cooperatives, schooling for peasants, fair wages and an end to nepotism, and quietly criticises the regime's drift into clan rule. It looks to European Christian labour movements rather than to either bloc. Its leverage lies in the paper's wide readership in the hills and the protection of the Church.

4.name: Abanyeshuri b'i Moscou
4.text:
The Moscow Students are a small group of Rwandans returned from scholarships at Soviet and East European universities, including Patrice Lumumba University, and their friends among young teachers and clerks. They meet discreetly in Kigali and Butare, wary of a regime that sees communism as the ally of the Tutsi exiles.

They argue that the Hutu revolution stopped halfway and that only planned development, state farms and an alliance with the socialist camp can end rural poverty. They condemn Belgian influence and the power of the Church. Their leverage is slight, but they are educated, connected to Soviet embassies in the region and able to reach student circles.

5.name: Abanyeshuri b'i Butare
5.text:
The Butare Students are the restless young people of the National University of Rwanda, founded in Butare in 1963, and of the secondary schools of the south. Influenced by May 1968, anti-colonial literature and Third World revolutions, they debate Fanon, Mao and Che in their residences.

They denounce the corruption and clannishness of the Kayibanda regime, the conservatism of the Church and dependence on Belgian aid, and call for a radical social revolution. They lack an organisation or a leader, and many will soon be absorbed into the state. Their leverage lies in their place as the country's future elite and their ability to start protests.

6.name: Union Nationale Rwandaise
6.text:
The Rwandese National Union was founded in 1959 by Tutsi chiefs and young nationalists loyal to the monarchy, demanding immediate independence from Belgium. Defeated in the 1961 elections, it was outlawed inside Rwanda and now survives among refugees in Uganda, Burundi, Tanzania and the Congo.

UNAR combines monarchist conservatism with anti-colonial radicalism and has received support from China and the socialist camp. It rejects the Hutu republic as a Belgian creation and demands the return of refugees and the king. Its base lies in refugee camps and the exile intelligentsia, and its leverage rests on armed bands on Rwanda's borders.

7.name: Abakiga
7.text:
The Abakiga are the northern Hutu of Gisenyi and Ruhengeri, whose officers, officials and notables resent the southern Nduga clique around Kayibanda. Proud of never having fully submitted to the old Tutsi kingdom, they dominate the officer corps of the National Guard.

They favour a hard, disciplined authoritarian state without the sentimental Catholic paternalism of the south, sceptical of foreign advice and determined to share power and resources. They are not openly organised, but their leverage lies in the army, where northerners hold key commands, and in a regional solidarity that could turn the guns of the National Guard against the presidency.

8.name: Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaat of Kigali
8.english: Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaat of Kigali
8.text:
The Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaat of Kigali is the small community of Twelver Shia traders of Indian origin settled in Kigali and Butare, linked to the Federation of Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaats of Africa based in East Africa. They run shops, transport and import houses.

The Jamaat focuses on religious education, mourning ceremonies, charity and mutual aid, and keeps a careful distance from politics. It looks to Shia scholars in Iraq and India for guidance. Its leverage lies in commercial capital and family networks stretching to Kampala, Nairobi and Dar es Salaam, on which Rwanda's import trade partly depends.

9.name: Wafuasi wa Najaf
9.text:
The Followers of Najaf are a tiny circle of young Shia traders and students in Kigali who look to the senior clerics of Najaf, above all Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim, for religious authority. They receive books and preachers from Iraq and East Africa.

They call for strict observance of Islamic law, the authority of the learned clergy over the community and resistance to secularism and Western influence. In Rwanda they have no political weight, but their leverage lies in links to wealthier Shia communities of East Africa and in the zeal of a small group convinced that Islam must guide public life.

10.name: Abayisilamu b'i Nyamirambo
10.text:
The Muslims of Nyamirambo are the Swahili-speaking community of Kigali's oldest Muslim quarter and of the trading centres of Rwamagana, Gisenyi and Butare. Descended from coastal traders and Rwandan converts, they gather around their imams and Quranic schools.

Their elders practise a quiet, conservative Sunni Islam, loyal to the government and focused on education, worship and recognition alongside the Christian churches. They want Muslim holidays respected, access to schools without forced conversion and support for pilgrimage. Their leverage lies in their importance in urban trade, transport and crafts, and in their good relations with Muslim states and East African communities.

11.name: Abahamagazi ba Kalifa
11.text:
The Callers to the Caliphate are a handful of young Rwandan Muslims who studied in Egypt and Saudi Arabia and returned with pan-Islamic writings. They gather in private homes in Nyamirambo, far from the attention of the authorities.

They denounce Muslim marginalisation under a Catholic state, reject nationalism and both blocs, and dream of a worldwide Muslim community under a restored caliphate and Islamic law. Their influence is minimal and they have no recognised leader. Their leverage lies only in the frustration of young Muslims excluded from Catholic schools and state jobs, and in the money and literature that flow from abroad.

12.name: Ishyirahamwe ry'Abayisilamu
12.text:
The Muslim Association is a circle of educated Rwandan Muslims, teachers and traders in Kigali who want to modernise their community. They draw on Egyptian reformist literature and preachers from East Africa, combining Islamic piety with the demand for modern education.

They call for Muslim schools, scholarships, legal recognition of Islam alongside the churches and a moral renewal of public life against corruption. They avoid confrontation with the government but criticise the Catholic monopoly on education. Their leverage lies in their education and in their role as the community's spokesmen in dealings with ministries and foreign Muslim donors.

13.name: Mouvement Démocratique Républicain–Parmehutu
13.english: Party of the Hutu Emancipation Movement
13.native_full: Mouvement Démocratique Républicain–Parti du Mouvement de l'Émancipation Hutu
13.text:
The MDR-Parmehutu grew from the Hutu Social Movement founded in 1957 by Grégoire Kayibanda and became the party of the 1959 revolution and the 1961 republic. De facto the only party since 1965, it re-elected Kayibanda unopposed in 1969 and controls the government, parliament and every commune.

The party presents itself as the voice of the Hutu majority, defending the republic against the return of the monarchy and Tutsi exiles. It is Catholic, rural and pro-Western, relying on Belgian aid and missionary support. Its base lies among Hutu peasants and southern officials, and its leverage rests on its monopoly of power, the bourgmestres and the National Guard.

14.name: Église Presbytérienne au Rwanda
14.text:
The Presbyterian Church in Rwanda is the largest Protestant church in the country, independent since 1959 after decades of German and Belgian Protestant missions. Alongside the Anglican and Baptist communities it represents a Protestant minority overshadowed by the Catholic establishment.

The Protestant churches stand for evangelical piety, moral discipline, schooling and health care in the hills, and keep their distance from both the ruling party and the blocs. They seek equal treatment with the Catholic Church in education. Their base lies in rural parishes and among teachers and nurses, and their leverage rests on their schools, clinics and ties with churches in Europe and America.

15.name: Travail, Fidélité, Progrès
15.text:
Trafipro was founded in 1956 as a Catholic consumer and coffee cooperative, with Grégoire Kayibanda among its early leaders. Since independence it has grown into a commercial giant with stores across the country and a near-monopoly on coffee buying and the distribution of basic goods.

Its managers, directors and their political patrons in Gitarama form the core of a new business elite tied to the ruling party. They defend state favours, monopoly licences and access to foreign credit. Their leverage lies in their control of the coffee trade, Rwanda's main export, and of consumer goods supply in the hills, which makes them indispensable to the regime.

16.name: Les Négociants de Gisenyi
16.text:
The Gisenyi Traders are the independent merchants, transporters and smugglers of the lake town of Gisenyi and its twin Goma across the Congolese border, joined by traders in Kigali and Butare. Among them are Rwandans of all origins, Swahili Muslims and Asian shopkeepers.

They want free movement of goods across borders, low taxes and an end to the privileges of Trafipro and party favourites. They are wary of the state and hostile to monopolies and controls. Their leverage lies in their role in supplying the north and the cross-border trade with Kivu, which brings goods and money that the official economy cannot provide.

17.name: Karisoke Research Center
17.text:
The Karisoke Research Center was founded in September 1967 by the American primatologist Dian Fossey on the slopes of the Virunga volcanoes, in Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park. Her team studies the mountain gorillas and fights poachers and cattle herders encroaching on the forest.

The conservationists demand strict protection of the park, the end of poaching and land clearing, and international support for wildlife protection. They clash with local farmers and officials who see the forest as land for settlement. Their leverage lies in international scientific prestige, the backing of the National Geographic Society and the world's growing fascination with the gorillas.

18.name: Association pour la Promotion Sociale de la Masse
18.english: Association for the Social Promotion of the Masses
18.native_full: Association pour la Promotion Sociale de la Masse
18.text:
The Association for the Social Promotion of the Masses was founded in 1957 by Joseph Gitera in Astrida, now Butare, as the first party to demand the emancipation of the Hutu peasantry. Overshadowed by Parmehutu after 1960, it faded and was absorbed into the single-party system, though Gitera remains a known figure.

APROSOMA's tradition calls for land reform, the abolition of feudal labour, schooling for the poor and a fair share of power for the southern peasantry. It looks to neither bloc. Its base lies among peasants and petty notables of Butare, and its leverage rests on southern resentment of Gitarama's dominance within the ruling party.

19.name: Inyenzi
19.text:
The Inyenzi are the armed bands of Tutsi exiles who have raided Rwanda from Burundi, Uganda and the Congo since 1961, most notably in the Bugesera offensive of December 1963. Their name, meaning cockroaches, comes from their night attacks. By 1970 their raids have largely ceased, but the networks remain.

Inspired by Chinese doctrines of people's war and supported for a time by Beijing, they seek to overthrow the Hutu republic and return the refugees. They are divided between monarchists and radicals. Their base lies in refugee camps, and their leverage rests on the exile youth and the regime's fear of a new incursion.

20.name: Rubanda Nyamwinshi
20.text:
Rubanda Nyamwinshi, the majority people, is the slogan of the Hutu revolution and the rallying cry of the party's hardliners, from local bourgmestres to propagandists who drafted the spirit of the 1957 Bahutu Manifesto. They hold that the republic belongs to the Hutu majority alone.

They demand quotas against Tutsi in schools and jobs, no return of refugees and vigilance against the exiles and their supposed collaborators within. They distrust intellectuals and foreigners alike. Their base lies among rural party militants and local officials, and their leverage rests on their capacity to mobilise the hills whenever Tutsi exiles threaten the republic.

21.name: Abarwanashyaka
21.text:
The Abarwanashyaka are the militant youth and activists of the ruling party who carried out the killings of Tutsi during the 1959 revolution and after the Bugesera raid of 1963. They form informal squads attached to communes and party cells.

They preach the defence of the Hutu revolution by any means, the expulsion of Tutsi influence from public life and total loyalty to the party. They despise both the Western liberals and the communists. Their base lies among unemployed young men in the hills, and their leverage rests on their readiness to use violence on command and on the protection of local officials.

22.name: Garde Nationale Rwandaise
22.text:
The Rwandan National Guard is the small army created with Belgian help at independence and commanded by Juvénal Habyarimana, a northern officer who has served as Minister of the National Guard and Police since 1965. It repelled the Inyenzi raids and remains the regime's main instrument of force.

The officer corps values order, discipline and national unity, distrusts the corruption and regionalism of politicians and cooperates closely with Belgian military advisers. Northern officers dominate its ranks. Its leverage lies in its monopoly of arms in a small country and the growing gap between its commanders and the southern civilian elite of Gitarama.

23.name: Abanyiginya
23.text:
The House of Abanyiginya is the dynasty that ruled the Kingdom of Rwanda for centuries until the monarchy was abolished in 1961. Its head, Mwami Kigeli V Ndahindurwa, crowned in 1959 and deposed by the referendum of 1961, lives in exile in East Africa.

The royalists call for the return of the king, the refugees and their land, and the restoration of national unity under the drum Kalinga and its traditions. Their base lies among Tutsi refugees, former chiefs and ritualists, and their leverage rests on a dynasty still revered by many exiles and on the diplomatic contacts of the monarchist movement abroad.
